  2. Your original Round 1 review
  3. The authors' point-by-point response

In your updated review, explicitly state which concerns have been adequately addressed and which remain outstanding. Be specific.

## Paper

## Abstract

The activation and valorization of inert molecules (e.g., dinitrogen (N ), alkanes, and alkenes) for the
synthesis of nitrogen-containing organic compounds have long been a highly sought-after goal in
chemistry. However, it remains a formidable challenge, stemming from the inherent chemical inertness
of the robust N≡N and C-H bonds, as well as the competitive adsorption and activation of reactants.
Consequently, examples of direct C-N bond formation using N and alkanes/alkenes as feedstocks
2
remain exceptionally scarce. Herein, we report that sodium hydride supported on magnesium oxide
(NaH/MgO) possesses unique multiple reactive sites, which enable the conversion of N and
2
unactivated arenes and facilitate C-N bond formation. The synergistic interplay between sodium,
magnesium, and hydride species at the NaH/MgO interface plays a pivotal role in the reduction of N
2
to NH species. These reactive NH intermediates then deprotonate the aryl C-H bond, attack the
x x
alkali-interacted aryl ring, and drive the formation of sodium anilide on the surface. Subsequent
protonation of sodium anilide yields aniline with high selectivity (>90%). This work demonstrates the
feasibility of transforming N and simple arenes into key nitrogen-containing organic compounds via a
2
solid surface-mediated process, thereby opening ample room for developing heterogeneous catalysts
for the transformation of N and organic substrates.
2

---

## Introduction

The direct transformation of N into value-added nitrogen-containing products poses a formidable
2
scientific challenge because of its inert nature. At present, almost all organic nitrogen-containing
compounds are synthesized using ammonia or amine as the nitrogen source. The well-established
industrial ammonia synthesis process (Haber-Bosch process) is energy intensive and of high carbon
footprint. In recent years, on one hand, the development of more efficient catalysts for ammonia
synthesis and alternative N fixation methods such as electrochemical, photochemical, plasma-
2
catalytic, and chemical looping routes have been received much attention1-6. On the other hand, the
direct transformation of N into organic nitrogen-containing compounds including amines, nitriles,
2
alkaloids etc., has also piqued significant interest7-12. Although heterogeneous, homogeneous, and
biological catalysts are known for their roles in catalytic nitrogen fixation to ammonia, the (catalytic)
synthesis of more complex nitrogen-containing organic molecules has far less precedent.

The pioneering research efforts regarding the conversion of N into organic compounds have
2
largely concentrated on molecular transition metal complexes because of their versatile and well-
defined compositions and structures, flexible chemical environments, as well as diversified
coordination modes for both N and organic substrates8,13-19. Although there are some cases of the
2
coupling of N with aryllithium or aryl halides, mediated by transition metals, to yield N-containing
2
compounds20-23, research on the reactions of N with arenes without prior functionalization remains
2
scarce. Holland et al. reported an iron β-diketiminate complex that mediates the coupling of N and
2
arenes to yield aniline derivatives24. The key C-N bond formation step occurs after partial silylation of
coordinated N on the Fe site. Tian et al. reported a plasma-enabled, catalyst-free approach to the
2
direct coupling of benzene and N into arylamines at the plasma-liquid interface, leveraging the high-
2
energy environment for N activation25. Very recently, Wei and Xi et al. reported a chromium-mediated
2
synthetic cycle for the direct conversion of N into multi-substituted hydrazines via aryl migration, here
2
termed the Xi Cycle, thereby representing a landmark advance in N functionalization26. The synthesis
2
of organic nitrogen-containing compounds from N and inert hydrocarbon sources on a solid surface,
2
hitherto, has rarely been reported.

Metal hydrides, existing in diverse structural and compositional forms, have played crucial roles
in many fundamental chemical transformations27-30. It has recently been demonstrated that alkali and
alkaline earth metal hydrides, including lithium hydride (LiH), barium hydride (BaH ), and sodium
2
hydride (NaH), can enable N fixation and subsequent hydrogenation to form N-H bonds, driven by
2
thermal energy, plasma, or ultraviolet light illumination31-35. Beyond N activation, hydride species (H‾)
2
have also been shown to mediate the activation of inert C-H bonds, such as that in benzene, under
mild conditions36-38. Taken together, these insights suggest the potential of hydrides to enable the
synergistic activation of N≡N and C-H bonds, thereby facilitating direct C-N bond formation. Herein,
we demonstrate the direct construction of C-N bond from inert N and unactivated arenes mediated
2
by sodium hydride supported on MgO. This transformation proceeds through three key steps: N
2
fixation via mechanochemistry, C-N bond formation under thermochemical conditions, and protonation
or hydrogenation to yield aniline. Anilines are obtained as dominant products with high selectivity
(>90%). Notably, the one-pot synthesis of nitrogen-containing organic compounds from N and simple
2
arenes can also be achieved under heating at 200°C. Different from molecular transition metal
complexes reported previously, this study reveals the intriguing role of alkali (and alkaline earth) metal
hydrides in the activation of N≡N and C-H bonds, along with the formation of the C-N bond.
Interestingly, the introduction of iron species exerts a pronounced promotional effect on N≡N bond
activation and subsequent C-N bond construction. This work could create substantial opportunities for
the advancement of heterogeneous materials aimed at converting N and hydrocarbon sources into
2
valuable organic nitrogen-containing compounds.

---

## Results

N fixation by NaH/MgO
2
While neat NaH has been reported to fix a negligible amount of N species under normal thermal
2
conditions33, we found that when dispersed on the MgO support, it is capable to fix N . Firstly, we
2
investigated thermal N fixation by NaH/MgO, which was prepared by ball-milling a mixture of NaH
2
(10wt%) and MgO powders in a commercial tungsten carbide (WC) jar. The N -temperature-
2
programmed reaction (N -TPR) profile of NaH/MgO shows H formation upon heating under a N flow,
2 2 2
with a signal intensity significantly higher than that in Ar-temperature-programmed decomposition
reaction (Ar-TPD) (Figure S1a), indicating N reduction by the hydride material31,39. In contrast, control
2
experiments confirmed that bare MgO produced no detectable H signal (Figure S1b). Moreover, the
2
NaH/MgO sample collected after heating in an N atmosphere exhibits the significant N-H bond
2
stretching vibrations at 3263 and 3217 cm-1 (Figure S2), confirming the formation of surface NH (x=1,
x
2) species. These results show that the ball-milled NaH/MgO can activate N and promote its
2
hydrogenation to form N-H bonds.

To simplify precursor preparation for N fixation, we explored a streamlined, one-pot process using
2
readily available Na metal pellets and MgO powder under H and N pressures to afford the N-fixed
2 2
samples. That is, Na, and MgO were co-feed and ball milled in a WC jar with variable N /H
2 2
pressures,
affording a solid product (denoted as Na-N-H/MgO). The X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern (Figure S3),
high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) image, and
energy-dispersive X-ray (EDX) mapping (Figure 2a) showed that Na species is evenly dispersed on
the MgO support at the (sub)nanometer scale. Diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform (DRIFT)
spectra (Figure 2b) showed several bands around 3277, 3244, and 3220 cm-1 which are assigned to
stretching vibrations of NH (x=1 and 2) species, a clear indication of N≡N bond cleavage followed by
x
hydrogenation to N-H bonds. Isotope experiments using 15N and D also confirmed that these bands
2 2
can be assigned to the stretching vibrations of NH (Figure S4). Noted that the observed vibrational
x
modes closely resemble those of NaNH and Mg(NH ) albeit with slight shifts, suggesting that the
2 2 2
NH species could be bonded with both Na and Mg atoms on the surface. Time-of-flight secondary-
x
ion mass spectrometry (ToF-SIMS) with negative mode (Figure 2c) detected cluster ions containing
NH species (NH‾, NaNH‾, NaNH ‾, and MgNH ‾), confirming NH formation and N bonding with Na
x 2 2 x
and/or Mg.

The amount of fixed nitrogen over Na-N-H/MgO was further quantified via hydrolysis with water
vapor, where protonation of the fixed nitrogen yielded NH as the sole N-containing product (Figure
3
S5); for example, after ball milling under a N (15 bar)-H (15 bar) atmosphere, the amount of fixed
2 2
nitrogen was determined to be 0.35 mmol g-1 (Figure S6b). Additionally, we observed that the
adventitious Fe introduced from the milling jar material significantly affects the amount of nitrogen fixed
during ball milling. As shown in Figures 2d and S6a, the amount of fixed nitrogen reaches 1.2 mmol g-
1 in a stainless-steel jar, approximately 3 times that in a WC jar. The XRD pattern reveals the presence
of Fe nanoparticles after ball-milling of Na and MgO in a stainless-steel jar (Figure S7). It is well-known
that Fe metal is catalytically active for ammonia synthesis from N and H . We therefore propose iron
2 2
species plays an important role in this system, and accordingly prepared the nitrogen-fixed material
comprising Na/MgO and Fe (denoted as Na-N-H/MgO-Fe). The amount of fixed N increases with
2
increasing N partial pressure, with a maximum of 2.17 mmol g-1 achieved over the Na/MgO-Fe sample
2
under N (25 bar)-H (10 bar) conditions (Figure 2d). These results demonstrate the efficacy of one-pot
2 2
mechanochemical methods in boosting N activation and conversion by NaH/MgO.

Coupling of fixed nitrogen species with benzene
We then examined the reaction of fixed NH species with benzene to see whether C-H bond activation
x
and C-N bond formation could take place. The Na-N-H/MgO-Fe samples were reacted with benzene
at 200 °C for 3 hours. The solid products were partially dissolved in DMSO, and the resulting solution
was analyzed by proton nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR) (Figure 3a). Distinct up-field chemical
shifts were observed at 5.35, 5.77, and 6.37 ppm, compared to typical aniline signals (6.48, 6.55, and
6.99 ppm). Similar proton resonance was observed in sodium anilide (C H -NHNa)40,41 (Figure S8),
6 5
which was synthesized via the reaction of NaH with aniline. These results indicate the formation of
sodium anilide salt species on the surface of Na-N-H/MgO-Fe. Moreover, the negative ToF-SIMS
spectrum (Figure S9) showed the formation of a series of C-N bond-containing species such as
C H NNa‾ and C H N‾ etc., further verifying the formation of anilide salts on Na-N-H/MgO.
6 5 6 5
The resulting anilide salts were further protonated with aqueous solutions, and the organic
products were extracted into organic solvents. GC-MS analysis identified aniline as the predominant
nitrogen-containing product, accompanied by the formation of other N-containing compounds
including phenylenediamine, aminobiphenyl, and benzidine, as well as the homocoupling side product
biphenyl (Figure S10).

Notably, Na-N-H/MgO sample synthesized in a WC jar (without Fe) also produced aniline via
reaction with benzene followed by protonation, albeit with a lower yield of 1.41 μmol g-1 (Figure 3b).
This result substantiates that Na-N-H/MgO is intrinsically capable of mediating C-H bond activation
and C-N bond formation in the absence of transition metals. In contrast, the reference Fe-N-MgO
sample without NaH failed to produce aniline upon reaction with benzene, underscoring the critical
role of the NaH/MgO interface in activating the arene C-H bond and enabling C-N bond formation.
Remarkably, when Fe was present, the Na-N-H/MgO achieved an aniline yield of 214 μmol g-1 at
200 °C (Figure 3b and Table S1). The specific prominent role of iron or other transition metals will be
investigated in a separate study.

The reaction of Na-N-H/MgO-Fe samples with benzene was conducted at different temperatures
(Figures 3c, 3d, and S11). Figure 3c reveals a volcano-shaped correlation between the amount of fixed
nitrogen and the reaction temperature, with the maximum at 200 °C. Lower conversion at higher
temperatures may be attributed to the decomposition of NH or decomposition/conversion of anilide
x
salts. Figure S11b shows the product distribution after reactions conducted at different temperatures.
Notably, the selectivity for total N-containing products was higher than 95% below 200 °C (Figure
S11a). More interestingly, the selectivity of aniline among N-containing products exceeded 90%
typically below 180 °C (Figure 3d), whereas aniline selectivity declined at higher temperatures,
suggesting over-reactions between benzene and the solid surface. Through the optimization of
reaction temperature, ball milling time, and loading of Na, a maximum conversion (ca. 26.3%) of fixed
N in the 10 wt% Na/MgO sample was achieved at 200 °C (Figure 3c and Table S1). The yields of
aniline and total N-containing compounds were 214 and 310 μmol g-1, respectively. Furthermore, to
verify aniline originated from N rather than nitrogen contaminates, Na-15N-H/MgO-Fe was
2
synthesized using 15N , and then reacted with benzene under the same conditions. GC-MS analysis
2
confirmed 15N-labelled aniline as the main product (Figure 3e), confirming N as the nitrogen source.
2

While hydrolysis offers a straightforward route to convert anilide salts to aniline, it results in the
concomitant hydration of Na/MgO, leading to loss of reactivity. This prompted us to explore
hydrogenation of anilide salts to produce aniline and regenerate NaH/MgO, potentially completing the
synthetic cycle. To verify this, neat sodium anilide was synthesized and subjected to hydrogenation
under a H flow. As shown in Figure 3f, sodium anilide undergoes the desorption of unreacted aniline
2
at lower temperature (ca. 80 °C), followed by hydrogenation to release additional aniline upon heating
to 275 °C. In contrast, Ar-TPD confirmed only the lower-temperature aniline desorption signal,
validating the hydrogenation process (Figure S12). Similarly, the surface-bonded sodium anilide
species on Na/MgO can also be hydrogenated to aniline, albeit with lower signal intensity. No aniline
formation was observed under argon atmosphere shown in Figure S13. These observations highlight
the potential to close the chemical cycle via hydrogenation treatment, warranting further investigation
to fully explore this process.

Conversion of N and benzene
2
Building on the successful stepwise synthesis of surface anilide, we further investigated the feasibility
of one-pot C-N bond formation. NaH/MgO-Fe samples were employed as the mediator, over which
benzene and N were introduced at specific pressures in a sealed system at 200 °C (Figure S14).
2
Aniline was obtained after protonation treatment, albeit with relatively low yield of 109 μmol g-1 under
20 bar N pressure, attributed to competitive adsorption of benzene and N on NaH/MgO-Fe.
2 2
Additionally, the one-step reaction was further evaluated in a flow reactor, where N served as both
2
the reactant gas and the carrier gas to bring benzene vapor to the NaH/MgO-Fe. Aniline was formed
after reaction at 200 °C under ambient pressure, followed by hydrolysis treatment (Figure S15). Overall,
the results present a pioneering protocol for the direct formation of C-N bonds from N and benzene,
2
in particular providing a viable strategy for the one-step transformation of N and arenes into nitrogen-
2
containing organic compounds.

Mechanistic studies
The reaction mechanism of Na/MgO for the activation of N and C H , as well as the subsequent C-N
2 6 6
bond formation was investigated by DFT calculations. Since neither NaH nor MgO alone functions for
this process, the synergy between NaH and MgO is crucial for activating H , N , and C H molecules,
2 2 6 6
as well as for facilitating C-N bond formation. TEM and ToF-SIMS results, revealed the presence of
sub-nanosized sodium cluster (Na -Na ) species (Figure S16). DFT calculation results further
1 5
indicated that a Na cluster model featuring a quasi-square planar geometry exhibits the optimal
4
interfacial binding energy, significantly superior to that of the Na -Na and Na clusters (Figure S17).
1 3 5
Accordingly, the Na /MgO(100) model was selected for the subsequent mechanistic study (Figure
4
S18).

On the Na /MgO model, H undergoes heterolytic dissociation into Na-H-Mg and O-H species,
4 2
with an energy barrier of merely 0.22 eV. N preferentially adsorbs in a side-on configuration at the
2
Na-Mg-Na triangular site, with the N-N bond elongated to 1.17 Å. Subsequently, the hydride at the Na-
H-Mg ensemble transfers to the adsorbed N , producing the *N H intermediate by 1.45 eV via a
2 2
reductive protonation pathway. Migration of surface *OH species to the Na-Mg site to regenerate Na-
H-Mg is exothermic; this replenishment of hydride facilitates the subsequent hydrogenation of *N H to
2
*N H , ultimately forming the surface species Na-NH -Mg and Na-N-Mg. These findings are supported
2 2 2
by experimental results from DRIFTS and ToF-SIMS.

After N fixation at the Na-H-Mg interface, benzene preferentially adsorbs at surface Na sites via
2
cation-π interaction, adopting an η6 configuration. Deprotonation of benzene occurs upon attack by *N
species, generating a surface-stabilized absorbed phenyl species on the Na-cluster surface (denoted
as Na-C H *) and Na-NH-Mg species. This step is significantly exothermic (ΔE = −1.00 eV) with a
6 5
moderate activation energy barrier (E = 0.36 eV), indicating favorable kinetics. Subsequently, surface
a
*C H was attacked by the nucleophilic *NH at the interface, yielding *C H NH . Subsequently,
6 5 2 6 5 2
*C H NH preferentially interacts with Na, accompanied by hydrogen transfer, to yield
6 5 2
thermodynamically stable C H NH-Na and OH species in strongly exothermic step (-0.87 eV).
6 5

Scope of arenes
The successful synthesis of aniline from N and benzene inspired us to investigate C-N bond formation
2
in reactions of N with a series of aromatic substrates bearing various functional groups using the
2
Na/MgO sample. As shown in Figure 4, a range of aniline derivatives were obtained under the general
reaction conditions. Monoalkylated arenes reacted with surface-bound NH species to afford the
x
corresponding amination products (2-11) in moderate to good yields. Meta-substituted N-containing
products predominate in these reactions, in contrast to conventional synthetic routes where
substitution typically occurs at the ortho- and para- positions, often guided by directing groups. For
example, m-toluidine (2) was the predominant product from toluene with a yield of 108 μmol g-1, with
trace amounts of p-toluidine (Figure S19). Arenes bearing ethyl, propyl and butyl groups similarly gave
exclusively meta-substituted amines (3-9) in appreciable yields, although their overall fixed-nitrogen
conversions were lower than those observed with benzene. The preference for reaction at electron-
deficient positions implies a process involving nucleophilic attack by NH species.
x

For bulkier arenes, 3-aminobiphenyl and 3-(2-phenylethyl) benzenamine (10 and 11) were
obtained in yields of 161 μmol g-1 and 81 μmol g-1, respectively. For dialkyl-substituted substrates, m-
xylene was converted to 3,5-dimethylaniline (12) with a relatively low yield of 22 μmol g-1. That is
attributed to electron-donating methyl groups enhancing the electron density of the aromatic ring,
thereby weakening its reactivity. In contrast, m-terphenyl afforded 3-amino-m-terphenyl (14) in a higher
yield of 93 μmol g-1. Despite lower yields, 1-aminofluorene (13) (13 μmol g-1) and 4-amino-p-terphenyl
(15) (12 μmol g-1) were also successfully synthesized. The amination method was also compatible with
polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. In these cases, naphthalene underwent amination at the β-position
(16). Similarly, both anthracene and phenanthrene underwent amination at β-sites (17 and 18), in
contrast to the typical electrophilic substitution patterns. Quinoline was also effectively transformed
into aminoquinoline (19) with a yield of 98 μmol g-1, consistent with the Chichibabin reaction pathway.
Reactions of halogenated benzenes with Na-N-H/MgO yielded aniline (20a-23a), diphenylamine (20b-23b), and triphenylamine (20c-23c) instead of the corresponding haloanilines, suggesting a
dehalogenative amination process analogous to the Buchwald-Hartwig cross-coupling42. Additionally,
the surface anilide salts can react with chlorotrimethylsilane (TMSCl) to afford silylated aniline
derivates (Figure S20).

---

## Methods

Chemicals and materials
Sodium block (99.7%) was purchased from Aladdin. MgO with a high specific surface area (ca. 170
m2 g-1) was synthesized according to a literature report43. Benzene (99.7%) was purchased from
Aladdin and then was dried by 3 Å zeolite before use. N (99.999%) and H (99.999%) were purchased
2 2
from Dalian Special Gas Co., Ltd. Ar (99.999%) was purchased from Dalian Junfeng Gases Co. Ltd.
15N (98%) was purchased from Cambridge Isotope Laboratories. All materials were handled inside a
2
glove box filled with purified argon (O , H O <1 ppm), owing to the air- and moisture-sensitivity of the
2 2
reagents and samples.

Materials synthesis
(1) Fabrication of Na/MgO
Na/MgO with a Na loading of 10 wt% was prepared as follows. The MgO was pretreated under an
argon flow at 580 °C for 8 h. Subsequently, metallic sodium (55.6 mg) and MgO (500 mg) were mixed
and ball milled in either a tungsten carbide jar or stainless-steel jar at 200 revolutions per minute (rpm)
for 12 hours.

(2) Fabrication of Na-N-H/MgO
Metallic sodium (55.6 mg) and MgO (500 mg) were mixed and ball milled in a tungsten carbide jar
under a N /H atmosphere at 200 rpm for 12 hours. The obtained sample was denoted as Na-N-
2 2
H/MgO.

(3) Fabrication of Na-N-H/MgO-Fe
Metallic sodium (55.6 mg) and MgO (500 mg) were mixed and ball milled in a stainless-steel jar under
a N /H atmosphere at 200 rpm for 12 hours. The obtained sample was denoted as Na-N-H/MgO-Fe.
2 2

(4) Fabrication of Fe-N/MgO
MgO (500 mg) was ball milled in a stainless-steel jar under a N /H atmosphere at 200 rpm for 12
2 2
hours. The obtained sample was denoted as Fe-N/MgO.

(5) Fabrication of NaH/MgO
NaH/MgO with a NaH loading of 10 wt% was also synthesized by ball milling NaH (44.4 mg) and MgO
(400 mg) in a tungsten carbide jar at 200 rpm for 8 hours.

After ball milling, the solid products were collected and stored in an Ar-filled glove box.

Quantification of fixed-N on Na-N-H/MgO samples
The active nitrogen species on Na-N-H/MgO were converted to ammonia by hydrolysis treatment and
quantified using a conductivity meter. Water vapor carried by argon was introduced into the reaction
tube to react with the Na-N-H/MgO. Then the exhaust gas was bubbled through dilute sulfuric acid,
and the change of the conductivity meter was tracked to determine the mounts of ammonia
discharge31,44,45, corresponding to the amount of nitrogen fixation of the sample.

General procedure of the reaction between Na-N-H/MgO and benzene
The reaction of Na-N-H/MgO with benzene was conducted in a home-made stainless-steel sealed
reactor with a quartz lining. In a typical experiment, 50 mg of Na-N-H/MgO and 200 μL of benzene
were added into the reactor in a glove box filled with argon. Then the reactor was heated to the desired
temperature for several hours (such as at 200 °C for 3 hours). After reaction, the solid-liquid mixtures
were collected for further characterization.

One-pot procedure for aniline synthesis
The one-pot reaction of benzene and N over Na/MgO was conducted in a custom-designed stainless-
2
steel sealed reactor with quartz lining. The Na/MgO was loaded into the quartz tube, while benzene
was introduced into the reactor outside the tube, and N pressurized to desired values. Once the
2

## Abstract

The activation and valorization of inert molecules (e.g., dinitrogen (N ), alkanes, and alkenes) for the
synthesis of nitrogen-containing organic compounds have long been a highly sought-after goal in
chemistry. However, it remains a formidable challenge, stemming from the inherent chemical inertness
of the robust N≡N and C-H bonds, as well as the competitive adsorption and activation of reactants.
Consequently, examples of direct C-N bond formation using N and alkanes/alkenes as feedstocks
2
remain exceptionally scarce. Herein, we report that sodium hydride supported on magnesium oxide
(NaH/MgO) possesses unique multiple reactive sites, which enable the conversion of N and
2
unactivated arenes and facilitate C-N bond formation. The synergistic interplay between sodium,
magnesium, and hydride species at the NaH/MgO interface plays a pivotal role in the reduction of N
2
to NH species. These reactive NH intermediates then deprotonate the aryl C-H bond, attack the
x x
alkali-interacted aryl ring, and drive the formation of sodium anilide on the surface. Subsequent
protonation of sodium anilide yields aniline with high selectivity (>90%). This work demonstrates the
feasibility of transforming N and simple arenes into key nitrogen-containing organic compounds via a
2
solid surface-mediated process, thereby opening ample room for developing heterogeneous catalysts
for the transformation of N and organic substrates.
2

---

## Introduction

The direct transformation of N into value-added nitrogen-containing products poses a formidable
2
scientific challenge because of its inert nature. At present, almost all organic nitrogen-containing
compounds are synthesized using ammonia or amine as the nitrogen source. The well-established
industrial ammonia synthesis process (Haber-Bosch process) is energy intensive and of high carbon
footprint. In recent years, on one hand, the development of more efficient catalysts for ammonia
synthesis and alternative N fixation methods such as electrochemical, photochemical, plasma-
2
catalytic, and chemical looping routes have been received much attention1-6. On the other hand, the
direct transformation of N into organic nitrogen-containing compounds including amines, nitriles,
2
alkaloids etc., has also piqued significant interest7-12. Although heterogeneous, homogeneous, and
biological catalysts are known for their roles in catalytic nitrogen fixation to ammonia, the (catalytic)
synthesis of more complex nitrogen-containing organic molecules has far less precedent.

The pioneering research efforts regarding the conversion of N into organic compounds have
2
largely concentrated on molecular transition metal complexes because of their versatile and well-
defined compositions and structures, flexible chemical environments, as well as diversified
coordination modes for both N and organic substrates8,13-19. Although there are some cases of the
2
coupling of N with aryllithium or aryl halides, mediated by transition metals, to yield N-containing
2
compounds20-23, research on the reactions of N with arenes without prior functionalization remains
2
scarce. Holland et al. reported an iron β-diketiminate complex that mediates the coupling of N and
2
arenes to yield aniline derivatives24. The key C-N bond formation step occurs after partial silylation of
coordinated N on the Fe site. Tian et al. reported a plasma-enabled, catalyst-free approach to the
2
direct coupling of benzene and N into arylamines at the plasma-liquid interface, leveraging the high-
2
energy environment for N activation25. Very recently, Wei and Xi et al. reported a chromium-mediated
2
synthetic cycle for the direct conversion of N into multi-substituted hydrazines via aryl migration, here
2
termed the Xi Cycle, thereby representing a landmark advance in N functionalization26. The synthesis
2
of organic nitrogen-containing compounds from N and inert hydrocarbon sources on a solid surface,
2
hitherto, has rarely been reported.

Metal hydrides, existing in diverse structural and compositional forms, have played crucial roles
in many fundamental chemical transformations27-30. It has recently been demonstrated that alkali and
alkaline earth metal hydrides, including lithium hydride (LiH), barium hydride (BaH ), and sodium
2
hydride (NaH), can enable N fixation and subsequent hydrogenation to form N-H bonds, driven by
2
thermal energy, plasma, or ultraviolet light illumination31-35. Beyond N activation, hydride species (H‾)
2
have also been shown to mediate the activation of inert C-H bonds, such as that in benzene, under
mild conditions36-38. Taken together, these insights suggest the potential of hydrides to enable the
synergistic activation of N≡N and C-H bonds, thereby facilitating direct C-N bond formation. Herein,
we demonstrate the direct construction of C-N bond from inert N and unactivated arenes mediated
2
by sodium hydride supported on MgO. This transformation proceeds through three key steps: N
2

or hydrogenation to yield aniline. Anilines are obtained as dominant products with high selectivity
(>90%). Notably, the one-pot synthesis of nitrogen-containing organic compounds from N and simple
2
arenes can also be achieved under heating at 200°C. Different from molecular transition metal
complexes reported previously, this study reveals the intriguing role of alkali (and alkaline earth) metal
hydrides in the activation of N≡N and C-H bonds, along with the formation of the C-N bond.
Interestingly, the introduction of iron species exerts a pronounced promotional effect on N≡N bond
activation and subsequent C-N bond construction. This work could create substantial opportunities for
the advancement of heterogeneous materials aimed at converting N and hydrocarbon sources into
2
valuable organic nitrogen-containing compounds.
